market_context: United States and Canada; practical, safety-first household guidance written natively for North American readers.
title: How Long Does Yogurt Last After Opening?

seo.title: How Long Does Yogurt Last After Opening?
seo.meta_description: Opened yogurt should stay cold and clean. Use the opening date, package condition, and spoilage signs instead of relying on the printed date alone.
seo.search_intent: Determine how long to keep opened yogurt and when time, temperature, or spoilage signs mean it should be discarded.

excerpt: Once yogurt is opened, the factory seal is no longer protecting it. The practical decision combines the opening date, continuous refrigeration, and the actual condition of the yogurt.
content_html:
A practical U.S. reference is about 1–2 weeks in the refrigerator for yogurt kept at 40°F (4°C) or below. Once the container is opened, however, do not treat that range as a brand-new two-week clock. Count the product's actual age, follow any shorter “use within X days of opening” instruction on the label, and discard it sooner if temperature control or condition is questionable.

That distinction matters with large tubs. A yogurt opened the day after purchase may have plenty of useful life left; one opened near the end of its recommended storage period does not gain another two weeks simply because the seal was broken later.

Use 1–2 weeks as an outer reference, then check the label

USDA consumer guidance lists yogurt at roughly 1–2 weeks refrigerated. A manufacturer can give a more specific after-opening recommendation based on its product, packaging, cultures, added fruit, or formulation. When the package says to finish it sooner after opening, use the shorter instruction.

Writing the opening date on a family-size container is useful because “I think we opened it recently” is not a storage method. If you genuinely cannot reconstruct when it was opened or whether it is already beyond the recommended period, replacing one tub is safer than guessing.

The printed date also needs context. Many food date labels are primarily about expected quality, not a stand-alone safety guarantee. What matters here is the combination of the recommended storage window, continuous refrigeration, clean handling, and the actual state of the yogurt.

Temperature can end the decision before the calendar does

Keep yogurt at 40°F (4°C) or below and return it to the refrigerator promptly after serving. Food-safety guidance says perishable foods that have been above 40°F for more than about 2 hours should be discarded; in very hot conditions above 90°F (32°C), that window is about 1 hour.

That rule is more important than whether the yogurt looks normal. A tub left on the counter through a long meal or forgotten in a warm car should not be put back in the refrigerator and given the rest of its original storage period.

Store yogurt on a consistently cold refrigerator shelf rather than relying on a warm spot in the door if your refrigerator has noticeable temperature swings. Close the lid firmly and avoid letting condensation, crumbs, or other foods fall into the container.

Normal whey separation is different from spoilage

A layer of clear or pale liquid on top is often whey that has separated from the yogurt. If the product is within its storage window, stayed cold, and otherwise looks and smells normal, that liquid can usually be stirred back in.

Visible mold is different: discard the whole yogurt. Yogurt is a high-moisture food, so removing only the visible spot is not a safe salvage method. Also discard a container with unexplained swelling or gas, a distinctly foul or yeasty odor, unusual discoloration, or a texture change that is not normal for that product.

Do not taste questionable yogurt as the deciding test. A small spoonful cannot prove that a product stayed at a safe temperature, and there is no benefit to tasting something that is already outside its known time or temperature limits.

Clean serving makes the opened tub easier to manage

Use a clean spoon each time, especially with a container that will be opened repeatedly over several days. Do not return a spoon that has been in someone's mouth or another food to the shared tub. Closing the lid promptly also reduces exposure to odors, spills, and contamination from the refrigerator.

Single-serving cups are simpler because most are eaten immediately after opening. With a large tub, portion what you need into a bowl rather than repeatedly leaving the whole container on the table.

Homemade yogurt and yogurt transferred to another container deserve the same basic controls: a clean covered container, a clear preparation or opening date, and continuous refrigeration. If a validated recipe or manufacturer gives a shorter storage period, follow it.

The useful answer is: think in roughly 1–2 weeks of total refrigerated storage, not “two fresh weeks after opening,” and let a shorter label instruction, excessive time out of refrigeration, mold, or clear spoilage end the window sooner.

faq.question: Does liquid on top mean yogurt is spoiled?
faq.answer: Not by itself. It is often separated whey. If the yogurt stayed cold and is within its storage window, stir it back in; mold, gas, swelling, or clearly abnormal odor or texture are different.

faq.question: Can I taste it to see whether it is safe?
faq.answer: Do not use tasting as a safety test if the yogurt was held too warm, is beyond a known storage window, or shows spoilage.

faq.question: Does using a clean spoon matter?
faq.answer: Yes. A clean utensil reduces outside contamination in a tub that may be opened repeatedly over several days.
